title: The TLS Protocol Version 1.0
summary: Specifies version 1.0 of Transport Layer Security, which gives communications privacy over the Internet. It is designed so client and server programs can talk in a way that prevents eavesdropping, tampering and message forgery. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 4346.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a secret tunnel for your messages. Nobody on the way can read or change what you send. This is the first version, and it is now old.

questions: how does tls protect internet traffic
how does the tls handshake work
what is the tls record protocol
subtitle: The first IETF standard for Transport Layer Security: private, tamper-evident connections between two applications.

tldr.problem: Two applications talking across the Internet need privacy and data integrity, and a way to authenticate each other, without every application inventing its own security.
tldr.mechanism: TLS 1.0 layers two protocols on a reliable transport: a Record Protocol that fragments, optionally compresses, MACs and encrypts data, and a Handshake Protocol that negotiates algorithms, authenticates peers and agrees on a shared secret.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2246 is Historic. It was obsoleted by RFC 4346 and was updated by several later RFCs.

today: RFC 2246 is Historic and was obsoleted by RFC 4346. It was also updated by RFC 3546, RFC 5746, RFC 6176, RFC 7465, RFC 7507 and RFC 7919, so it is no longer the current definition of TLS.

sections.title: Goals and Two-Layer Design
sections.content:
The primary goal of the TLS Protocol is privacy and data integrity between two communicating applications. It has two layers on top of a reliable transport such as TCP: the Record Protocol and the Handshake Protocol.

The Record Protocol keeps the connection private, using symmetric encryption whose keys are generated uniquely for each connection, and reliable, using a keyed MAC for message integrity. The Handshake Protocol lets the peers authenticate with public-key cryptography, negotiate a shared secret that eavesdroppers and even a man in the middle cannot obtain, and detect any tampering with the negotiation.

The goals in priority order are cryptographic security, interoperability, extensibility and relative efficiency. TLS is application protocol independent, but it deliberately does not say how an application starts a TLS handshake or interprets certificates. The document is based on SSL 3.0; the two are close but do not interoperate, though TLS 1.0 can back down to SSL 3.0.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two helpers. One packs each message in a locked, sealed box. The other helps both sides agree on the key and prove who they are before any box is sent.

sections.title: The Record Protocol
sections.content:
The Record Protocol takes data to send, fragments it into blocks, optionally compresses it, applies a MAC, encrypts it and transmits the result. Received data is decrypted, verified, decompressed and reassembled. Records carry a type (change_cipher_spec 20, alert 21, handshake 22 or application_data 23), a version, a length and the fragment. TLS 1.0 uses version { 3, 1 }, a historical value because it is a minor modification of SSL 3.0. A fragment carries at most 2^14 bytes.

Each direction has a connection state with a sequence number, starting at zero, that goes into the MAC so missing, extra or repeated records are detectable. The MAC is HMAC_hash over the sequence number, type, version, length and fragment, computed before encryption. Stream ciphers and CBC block ciphers are specified, with block padding of up to 255 bytes.

Keys, MAC secrets and IVs are all derived from the 48-byte master secret and the two 32-byte hello randoms, using a pseudorandom function (PRF) that mixes HMAC with both MD5 and SHA-1 so it stays secure if either hash remains secure.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message is cut into pieces, stamped with a number and a tamper seal, then locked in a box. The receiver unlocks each box, checks the seal and the number, and puts the pieces back together.

sections.title: The Handshake Protocol
sections.content:
The handshake agrees on a protocol version, picks algorithms, optionally authenticates the peers, creates a master secret and gives the security parameters to the record layer. The client sends ClientHello with its version, a random value, a session ID and its ordered list of cipher suites and compression methods. The server answers with ServerHello picking one of each, or a handshake_failure alert.

The server may then send its Certificate, a ServerKeyExchange and a CertificateRequest, and ends its part with ServerHelloDone. The client replies with its own certificate if asked, a ClientKeyExchange that sets the premaster secret, and a CertificateVerify where needed. Both sides then send ChangeCipherSpec followed by a Finished message, which proves both ended up with the same parameters and that nobody tampered with the handshake.

A client can name an earlier session ID. If the server agrees, an abbreviated handshake skips the key exchange and goes straight to ChangeCipherSpec and Finished. The server may return an empty session ID to say the session cannot be resumed.

Sending handshake messages out of order is a fatal error. Only HelloRequest, which the server may send at any time, is exempt.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like two spies meeting. They say hello, agree on a secret handshake, show their ID cards, and then each says a test phrase locked with the new code to prove it works. If they have met before, they can skip straight to the test phrase.

sections.title: Alerts and Closing a Connection
sections.content:
Alert messages carry a level, warning (1) or fatal (2), and a description such as bad_record_mac (20), handshake_failure (40), unknown_ca (48) or protocol_version (70). A fatal alert ends the connection immediately, and both sides must forget the session identifier, keys and secrets tied to it.

Either party can start a close by sending close_notify. This exists so the two sides know the connection is truly ending, which avoids a truncation attack. The session becomes unresumable if a connection ends without proper close_notify alerts.
sections.plainLanguage: If something goes badly wrong, one side shouts a warning and both hang up and forget the secret code. A polite goodbye lets each side know the call really ended and was not cut off by someone else.

sections.title: Mandatory Cipher Suite and Security Analysis
sections.content:
Unless an application profile says otherwise, a TLS compliant application MUST implement the cipher suite TLS_DHE_DSS_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA. The RFC's Security Considerations section is a single sentence saying security issues are discussed throughout the memo; Appendix F holds the security analysis.

That analysis says the channel is secure against man-in-the-middle attacks whenever the server is authenticated, while completely anonymous sessions are inherently vulnerable. The RFC warns that an attacker can still push peers toward weaker options, for example by blocking the port or trying to get an unauthenticated connection, so higher layers must know their own requirements and never send data over a channel weaker than they need. It singles out 40-bit encryption as suitable only for data worth no more than the effort to break it.

The document also describes a defense against version rollback: clients in SSL 2.0 compatibility mode set special padding bytes so TLS-capable servers can detect and reject the downgrade.
sections.plainLanguage: The rulebook says every grown-up TLS program must know at least one standard lock. It also warns that a sneaky person may try to trick both sides into using a weak lock, so you should never put something precious behind a flimsy one.
